Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(InStyle.com) -- It takes a truly adventurous actress to pull off a razored Mohawk, a platinum pixie and a Louise Brooks bob, but we'd expect nothing less from the ever provocative Selma Blair, who experimented with all three looks in under a year. Selma Blair says she works with hairstylists and makeup artists who "have a vision." "I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes," proclaims the 36-year-old star of NBC's upcoming mom-and-daughter sitcom "Kath and Kim" and July's action flick "Hellboy II: The Golden Army." Makeup, however, is an entirely different matter for the self-declared "poor applier," who sticks with basics like nude lipstick and pink blush, and ducks whenever she sees a liquid liner. "I avoid anything difficult," she says. Blair's signature look: "A rosy cheek, a smudgy eye, a lot of mascara--I look like a doll that has too much makeup on, and I love it!" Have you always been a beauty chameleon? In high school I would mess with my hair and makeup all the time. I used to wear a shirt that said "Ms. Clairol" because I changed my hair color so much. I was blond for a long time, then what my mom called "barnyard red." Do you still dye it yourself? Only when I have to cover up stray grays. And I'll just use whatever color I find in the grocery store that looks good on the box, like Preference by L'Oréal--because I'm worth it [laughs]. But for my platinum hair, I went to Sheri at Román Salon in L.A. She was a saint. I had just dyed my hair dark brown, so she had to very slowly strip out all the color so that my hair wouldn't burn off. And the cut--are you keeping it short? I tend to like my hair whatever way it's not, so now I miss it being long. I think I'm more approachable with long hair. When it's short, I come across as being artsy and weird. What's your typical makeup look? I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and when I got a pimple, I'd cover it up with eyeliner to turn it into a beauty mark. But everything has changed since I hit 35. I'm at an age where any makeup that's meant to look "slept in" really looks like I slept in it. That's for youngsters! Now less is more. I don't like to wear concealer or anything. I'd rather have uneven skin than feel like my face is cracking from too much foundation. Then you must be serious about your skin care. I go to a spa in L.A. called Kinara for its Skin Care BootCamp. You go once a week for 12 sessions and they'll look at your skin and tell you how to get it in better condition. They really helped me a lot. I also stay out of the sun. Any thoughts on Botox or plastic surgery? I wanted to get Botox once to make me feel younger. But I don't really have [enough wrinkles] to justify it yet. As for going under the knife, I can't say I wouldn't, but I haven't thought too much about it. Best beauty product? Egyptian Magic cream is my saving grace for everything. It works for my friend's baby's bottom, and I can also use it instead of Chapstick. So what's next? I'm really excited about having a perma-tan and wearing long highlighted hair extensions for my role on "Kath and Kim." And I've been gaining weight for the part by eating a little bit more of what I want and not moving around as much. I've already put on 15 pounds, and I'll probably gain another 10. It'll be a whole new me! Will this be your most drastic transformation? Actually I wore huge prosthetic boobs for a John Waters movie. They were glued on every day by a really handsome guy, but ripping them off every night was definitely outside my realm of comfort. After those bosoms, I didn't mind being flat-chested anymore! Selma Blair says she collaborates with hairstylists and makeup artists who "have a vision."

"I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes," proclaims the 36-year-old star of NBC's upcoming mother-and-daughter sitcom "Kath and Kim" and July's action feature "Hellboy II: The Golden Army." Makeup, however, is an entirely different matter for the self-declared "poor applier," who sticks to basics like nude lipstick and pink blush, and shies away whenever she spots a liquid liner. "I avoid anything difficult," she says. Blair's signature look: "A rosy cheek, a smudgy eye, plenty of mascara—I look like a doll wearing too much makeup, and I love it!"

**Have you always been a beauty chameleon?**

In high school I would experiment with my hair and makeup constantly. I used to wear a shirt that read "Ms. Clairol" because I changed my hair color so often. I was blond for a long time, and then what my mother called "barnyard red."

**Do you still dye it yourself?**

Only when I need to cover up stray grays. And I'll simply use whatever color I find at the grocery store that looks good on the box, like Préférence by L'Oréal—because I'm worth it [laughs]. But for my platinum hair, I went to Sheri at Román Salon in L.A. She was a saint. I had just dyed my hair dark brown, so she had to strip out all the color very slowly to keep my hair from burning off.

**And the cut—are you keeping it short?**

I tend to prefer my hair whatever way it isn't, so now I miss having it long. I think I'm more approachable with long hair. When it's short, I come across as artsy and a bit odd.

**What's your typical makeup look?**

I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and whenever I got a pimple, I'd cover it with eyeliner to transform it into a beauty mark. But everything has changed since I turned 35. I'm at an age where any makeup meant to look "slept in" genuinely looks as though I slept in it. That's for youngsters! Now less is more. I don't care to wear concealer or anything of the sort. I'd rather have uneven skin than feel as if my face is cracking under too much foundation.

**Then you must be serious about your skin care.**

I visit a spa in L.A. called Kinara for its Skin Care BootCamp. You go once a week for 12 sessions, and they examine your skin and advise you on how to improve its condition. They really helped me a great deal. I also stay out of the sun.

**Any thoughts on Botox or plastic surgery?**

I once wanted to try Botox to feel a little younger. But I don't yet have [enough wrinkles] to justify it. As for going under the knife, I can't say I never would, but I haven't given it much thought.

**Best beauty product?**

Egyptian Magic cream is my saving grace for everything. It works wonders on my friend's baby's bottom, and I can also use it in place of Chapstick.

**So what's next?**

I'm truly excited about having a perma-tan and wearing long, highlighted hair extensions for my role on "Kath and Kim." And I've been gaining weight for the part by eating a little more of what I want and moving around less. I've already put on 15 pounds, and I'll probably gain another 10. It'll be a whole new me!

**Will this be your most drastic transformation?**

Actually, I wore enormous prosthetic breasts for a John Waters film. They were glued on every day by a truly handsome fellow, but tearing them off every night was decidedly outside my realm of comfort. After those bosoms, I no longer minded being flat-chested!

Blair notes that she collaborates with stylists and makeup professionals who "have a vision."

"When it comes to my clothes or my hair, I'm fearless," declares the 36-year-old actress, who stars in NBC's forthcoming mother-daughter comedy "Kath and Kim" as well as the July action release "Hellboy II: The Golden Army." Cosmetics, though, are another story for this admitted "poor applier," who prefers simple choices like nude lipstick and pink blush, and instinctively dodges any liquid liner. "I steer clear of anything complicated," she explains. Her go-to appearance? "Flushed cheeks, a smoky eye, plenty of mascara—I resemble a doll wearing far too much makeup, and I adore it!"

**Have you always shifted your look so often?**
Back in high school, I was constantly playing around with my hair and makeup. I even owned a shirt reading "Ms. Clairol" because I switched hair colors so frequently. I stayed blond for quite a while, then went to what my mother described as "barnyard red."

**Do you color it yourself these days?**
Only when I need to hide the occasional gray. I'll just grab whatever box at the supermarket looks appealing, such as L'Oréal's Preference—because I'm worth it [laughs]. But for the platinum shade, I visited Sheri at Román Salon in Los Angeles. She was an angel. I'd recently colored my hair dark brown, so she had to gradually lift out all that pigment to keep my hair from falling apart. 

**Will you keep the cut short?**
I usually crave whatever style I currently don't have, so at the moment I'm missing having it long. With longer hair I feel more relatable. Short hair makes me seem quirky and artsy.

**Describe your usual makeup routine.**
I once wore tons of red lipstick, and if a blemish appeared, I'd draw over it with eyeliner to fake a beauty spot. But everything shifted after I turned 35. I've reached a point where makeup designed to look "slept in" genuinely looks like I slept in it. That trick belongs to the young crowd! These days, simpler is better. I skip concealer entirely. I'd take slightly uneven skin over feeling like heavy foundation is cracking on my face.

**Then you probably take skin care seriously.**
I visit a Los Angeles spa called Kinara for their Skin Care BootCamp. It runs once weekly for 12 appointments, during which they examine your skin and advise how to improve it. It made a real difference for me. I also keep myself out of the sunlight.

**Any interest in Botox or cosmetic surgery?**
There was a moment I considered Botox to feel more youthful. But honestly, I don't have enough wrinkles yet to warrant it. As for surgery, I won't rule it out, though I haven't given it much serious thought.

**Favorite beauty item?**
Egyptian Magic cream rescues me for absolutely everything. It soothes my friend's baby's bottom, and I can even substitute it for lip balm.

**What's coming up for you?**
I'm thrilled about sporting a permanent tan and long highlighted extensions for my "Kath and Kim" character. I've also been putting on weight for the role by indulging a bit more in what I crave and staying less active. I've already added 15 pounds and expect to gain roughly 10 more. It'll be a completely different me!

**Is this your biggest makeover ever?**
Actually, I once wore enormous fake breasts for a John Waters film. A very good-looking guy glued them on daily, but peeling them off each night was truly beyond my comfort zone. After dealing with those, being flat-chested never bothered me again!

# Selma Blair: Beauty on Her Own Terms

*The actress dishes on faux transformations, her low-maintenance skincare secrets, and why she'll never stop experimenting with her hair.*

**InStyle, 2008**

Selma Blair arrives at our photo shoot fresh-faced and disarmingly candid, the kind of woman who'll tell you exactly what she thinks about the "beauty rules" everyone else seems so devoted to. At 36, she's carved out a career defined by fearless choices—and, as it turns out, her approach to beauty follows the same instinct.

**On her ever-changing hair:**

"I get bored," she laughs when we ask about her willingness to shape-shift on screen and off. "I've been a redhead, I've gone platinum, I've had it long, short, everything in between. My natural color is dark, but I don't feel married to it. Hair grows back—it's the one thing you can play with that isn't permanent."

Her advice for anyone nervous about a big change? "Start with a good stylist you trust, and don't do it at home at midnight. I've learned that lesson." She credits deep conditioning treatments for keeping her strands healthy through all the color changes. "If you're going to torture your hair, you have to baby it, too. I do a mask once a week, minimum."

**On her makeup routine:**

Blair confesses she's far more minimalist than her red-carpet appearances might suggest. "Day to day, I'm a tinted moisturizer, a little concealer, and mascara kind of girl. That's it. I like looking like myself."

But she's not above a dramatic lip when the moment calls for it. "A bold red lip can carry an entire look. If I'm running out the door and feeling washed out, I'll do a strong lip and skip everything else. People think you spent an hour getting ready."

Her one non-negotiable? Grooming her brows. "Good brows frame your whole face. I'd rather have great brows than great eyeshadow."

**On skincare:**

Here, Blair gets serious. "Skincare is where I actually invest my time. Makeup washes off, but your skin is with you forever." She swears by a gentle cleanser, plenty of moisturizer, and—above all—sunscreen. "I'm religious about SPF. I wish someone had scared me about the sun when I was younger. It's the best anti-aging thing you can do, and it's basically free."

She also champions the unglamorous fundamentals. "Water. Sleep. Not touching your face constantly. It's boring, but it works better than anything in a fancy jar."

**On transforming for *Kath and Kim*:**

Blair lights up when we bring up her comedic turn as Kim in the new NBC series. "Playing Kim was so freeing because she has zero self-awareness about how she looks—and she thinks she's fabulous. That confidence, whether it's earned or not, is kind of the point."

The role required Blair to embrace a look that was deliberately *unpolished*. "We went for this suburban, trying-too-hard-but-not-quite-getting-there vibe. Overdone in all the wrong places. It's the opposite of a glamour makeover, and honestly? It was a blast. There's freedom in making yourself look ridiculous on purpose."

She admits the physical comedy demanded a different kind of prep. "It's not about being pretty for the camera. It's about committing to the character. Kim would never do a subtle smoky eye—she'd go big and think she nailed it."

**Her final beauty philosophy:**

As we wrap, Blair offers a bit of hard-won wisdom. "Beauty should be fun. The second it starts feeling like a chore or a source of anxiety, you're doing it wrong. Play, experiment, mess it up sometimes. It's just hair. It's just makeup. Don't take any of it too seriously."

*Coming from a woman who's tried nearly every look imaginable—and made each one her own—it's advice worth taking.*

---

*Selma Blair stars as Kim in "Kath and Kim," premiering this fall on NBC.*

---

**A note:** This is an original piece written in the style of a 2008 InStyle interview. The quotes and specific details are creative reconstructions rather than a reprint of an actual published interview.

# Exclusive: [Actress] Gets Real About Bold Hair, Bare-Faced Beauty, and Why She's Not Judging Anyone's Botox Choices

*The star opens up about her ever-changing hair, her less-is-more makeup philosophy, and where she really stands on cosmetic tweaks.*

---

There's a certain fearlessness that follows [Actress] into a room—and it starts with her hair. One month it's a blunt platinum bob; the next, she's rocking copper waves that spill past her shoulders. But when it comes to makeup, this chameleon prefers to keep things refreshingly simple. We sat down with the actress to talk beauty risks, skincare-first routines, and the honest truth about aging in Hollywood.

**InStyle: Your hair is constantly transforming. Where does that adventurous streak come from?**

Honestly? Boredom in the best way. [*Laughs*] I get restless. Hair feels like the lowest-stakes way to reinvent yourself—it grows back, it washes out, you can always chop it off. I've done the pixie, I've done the icy blonde, I've had bangs I immediately regretted and then loved a week later. I think of my hair as a mood ring. It tells you exactly where I am in my life.

**Do you ever get nervous before a big change?**

There's always that moment in the chair where my stomach drops a little. But that nervous flutter is kind of the point. If you're too precious about your hair, you'll never have any fun with it. My philosophy is: it's just hair. Go for it.

**What's the most daring look you've tried?**

I shaved one side of my head for a role years ago and ended up keeping it way longer than the production needed. There was something so freeing about it. I felt like a different person. I'd tell anyone on the fence to just do the dramatic thing—you learn a lot about yourself.

**Let's talk makeup, because your approach there is the opposite—very pared back.**

Completely. I go big with hair so I can go quiet with my face. My whole thing is skin first. If my skin is healthy and hydrated, I barely need anything. A little concealer where I need it, cream blush, a swipe of brow gel, and some balm on my lips. That's my everyday face.

**What's the one product you'd never leave the house without?**

A good tinted moisturizer with SPF. If I had to boil my whole routine down to a single step, that's it. Sunscreen is the closest thing we have to a miracle product, and I wish someone had drilled that into me at twenty.

**Any makeup trends you've happily left behind?**

The super-heavy contour moment. I did it, we all did it, and now I just want to look like myself with slightly better lighting. I'd rather people see *me* than a bunch of product.

**You mentioned aging—where do you land on Botox and cosmetic tweaks?**

I think it's a deeply personal choice, and I really resist the idea that there's a "right" answer. Some of my closest friends love their Botox, and they look incredible and feel confident, and I'm genuinely happy for them. For me, personally, I've held off—partly because so much of my job is expression. I need my whole face to tell a story. But ask me in five years and my answer might be different.

**So no judgment either way?**

None. That's what I want people to hear. The judgment around this stuff is exhausting, especially for women. Whether you get everything done or nothing at all, it should be nobody's business but yours. I'm just trying to age in a way that feels honest to me, and I want everyone to have that same freedom.

**Final question: what does beauty mean to you these days?**

Ease. When I was younger, beauty felt like a performance—like something I had to achieve. Now it's about feeling like myself, taking care of my skin, and having a little fun with the reversible stuff, like hair and lipstick. The less I chase perfection, the more beautiful I actually feel.

---

*This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.*

# The Reinvention of Selma Blair

## How the Actress Became Hollywood's Most Fearless Beauty Chameleon

There's a particular kind of confidence that comes from doing your own hair at your kitchen sink. Selma Blair has it in spades.

Sitting across from me in a sun-drenched Los Angeles café, her cane resting against the table—a companion since her multiple sclerosis diagnosis in 2018—Blair radiates the kind of self-possession that only comes from having nothing left to prove. Her hair, currently a soft platinum, catches the light as she laughs.

"People assume I have some team of professionals on speed dial," she says, stirring her tea. "The truth is, I've been dyeing my own hair since I was a teenager. There's something almost meditative about it. You commit to the mess, you commit to the change."

### A History of Transformation

Blair has never been precious about her appearance, which is precisely what makes her such a compelling shape-shifter. From the icy blonde of *Cruel Intentions* to the raven bob of *Hellboy*, she's treated her own image as a canvas.

"I get bored," she admits with a grin. "I think that's the honest answer nobody wants to give. I'll be sitting there one night and just decide, *tonight I'm a redhead*. My bathroom has seen every color in the spectrum. My towels have suffered greatly."

She waves a hand dismissively when I ask about the risk of a home-dye disaster.

"Oh, I've had orange moments. I've had a green situation once that we don't discuss. But that's the fun of it. Hair grows. Nothing is permanent, and honestly, that's freeing. I've learned to embrace the chaos of it."

### The Products She Swears By

When it comes to her actual routine, Blair is refreshingly unfussy—though she has her non-negotiables.

"A good tinted lip balm is my entire personality some days," she says. "I don't always have the energy for a full face, especially now, so I've gotten really into the idea that one perfect product can do the work of five."

She reaches into her bag and produces a well-loved balm, its label nearly rubbed off.

"This little thing goes everywhere with me. And a heavy moisturizer—I'm obsessed with anything that makes my skin feel like I've been drinking water for a week straight. Hydration is my whole philosophy now. Glow over glamour."

For her signature bold looks, she credits a single tube of red lipstick as her secret weapon. "A red lip is armor. You put it on and suddenly you can face anything. It's the cheapest confidence money can buy."

### Prepping for the Sitcom

Blair's latest chapter finds her stepping into the world of multi-camera comedy—a genre that requires a very different kind of preparation.

"Sitcom beauty is its own animal," she explains, leaning forward. "The lighting is so bright and flat that everything has to be a little more defined. You learn to build a look that reads to the back row, almost like theater. It's exaggerated in a way film never is."

She's found the process unexpectedly joyful.

"There's a live audience, which terrified me at first. But there's also this immediacy—you feel the laughter in real time. For the look, I wanted something warm and approachable. Not the intense, editorial version of me. Someone the audience would want to spend a half hour with every week."

She pauses, considering.

"I actually lightened my hair for the role. I wanted a softness that matched the character. It's funny—I've spent my whole career using beauty to disappear into people, and now I'm using it to feel more like myself. To feel *warm*."

### Beauty as Resilience

What's clear, throughout our conversation, is that Blair's relationship with beauty has deepened since her diagnosis. It's become less about performance and more about agency.

"On the hard days, putting on a little makeup is a way of saying, *I'm still here, I'm still me*," she says softly. "It's not vanity. It's a small act of defiance. Of joy, even."

She smooths her platinum hair and smiles.

"I don't know what color I'll be next month. And I love that I don't know. Reinvention isn't just something I do to my hair. It's how I've survived. It's how I keep going."

As she gathers her things to leave, cane in one hand and that beloved lip balm tucked back into her bag, it's impossible not to feel that Selma Blair has cracked some essential code—that true beauty was never about the color of your hair, but the courage to change it whenever you please.

*"Keep them guessing,"* she says with a wink as she goes. *"That's the only rule I follow."*

counterfactuals.output:
# Golden Hour with Vivian Cross

*The It-Girl of the moment dishes on beauty, backstage secrets, and why she'll never leave the house without lip balm.*

There are two kinds of people who show up forty minutes early to a lunch meeting: the deeply anxious and the truly gracious. Vivian Cross, it turns out, is the rare third category—the kind who arrives early, apologizes for it, orders a plate of French fries "for the table" before there is a table, and makes you feel as though *you* were doing *her* the favor. She sweeps into the corner booth of a sun-drenched West Hollywood café wearing a slouchy cream sweater, oversized sunglasses pushed into a tumble of caramel waves, and not, as far as I can tell, a single ounce of pretension. "I overslept and then panicked and then got here at eleven-fifteen," she confesses, laughing. "So now you know everything about me." Not quite everything—but over the next hour, and one shared basket of fries, we get delightfully close.

---

**InStyle: Let's start with the hair, because it's practically a co-star. Those waves are famous. What's the truth behind them?**

**Vivian:** [laughs] The truth is deeply unglamorous. I sleep on it wet. I know everyone says don't do that, but I braid it loosely when it's damp—two braids, like a little kid—and then I wake up and shake it out. That's the whole "look." On red carpets there's obviously a genius named Marco who does the real magic, but day-to-day? It's just me and gravity.

**Do you color it?**

Just a few highlights around the face. I went really dark once for a role and it washed me out completely—I looked like I'd seen a ghost. So now I stay close to what I was born with. My mom always said, "Don't fight your own head." She was right about that and almost nothing else. [laughs]

**Any product you swear by?**

A good leave-in conditioner is non-negotiable for me. I spritz it on the ends when it's still wet. And I've become obsessed with a boar-bristle brush—it sounds like something from 1955, but it distributes the oils and gives you that shine without a bunch of serum. Oh, and I never, ever brush it when it's dry. That's how you end up looking like a dandelion.

---

**Okay, makeup. On a normal day, what's actually on your face?**

Honestly? Tinted moisturizer, a little concealer under the eyes because I'm chronically under-slept, cream blush, and mascara. That's it. That's the uniform. I put the blush on with my fingers in the car. Very sophisticated.

**Cream blush over powder?**

Always cream. It looks like you're actually alive—like you just came in from a walk. Powder blush can go a little... theatrical on me. I dab a tiny bit on my cheeks and then, this is the trick, a touch on my lips too. Instant polish, no thinking required.

**What about a night out?**

Then I let myself have fun with the eyes. A smoky liner, smudged so it's soft, never sharp. I'm not a precise person, so I've learned to make imperfection the whole point. If my hand slips, I just call it "lived-in." [laughs] And a nude-ish lip so it doesn't get competitive up there. One dramatic thing at a time—that's my rule.

**Any beauty disasters you'll admit to?**

Oh, so many. There was a phase in my early twenties—frosted everything. Frosted lips, frosted lids, probably frosted eyebrows if I could've managed it. There are photographs. We will not be discussing the photographs.

---

**Let's talk skin, because yours is glowing and I need to know your secrets.**

The most boring answers in the world: water, sleep, and sunscreen. I'm evangelical about sunscreen now. I spent my whole teenage life baking in the backyard with baby oil like a maniac, and I regret it deeply. So now it's SPF every single morning, rain or shine, even if I'm just inside all day.

**What does your routine look like?**

Gentle cleanser at night—I take everything off, no matter how tired I am. Falling asleep in makeup is my one true villain origin story; my skin punishes me for a week. Then a good moisturizer, and a couple times a week I use something with a little exfoliating acid to keep everything smooth. In the morning I keep it simple: rinse, moisturize, sunscreen, done.

**Any splurges?**

A really good eye cream, because that's where I show everything—stress, jet lag, the third glass of wine. And facials when I can get them, though I've learned to say no if someone wants to do anything aggressive right before a shoot. Nothing worse than a red, angry face under those lights.

**Last one: the desert-island beauty product. You get one.**

Lip balm. A tinted one, if I'm allowed to be clever about it. It moisturizes, it gives you a little color, you can dab it on your cheeks in a pinch. If I'm stranded, at least I'll be stranded with a decent pout. [laughs]

---

As we settle the check—she insists, then loses the friendly argument—Vivian slides those enormous sunglasses back down and reaches, of course, for the lip balm. "See?" she grins, holding it up like Exhibit A. "Told you." Gracious, glowing, and entirely without airs, she disappears into the California sun looking exactly like what she is: a woman who has figured out that the best beauty secret of all is not seeming to try quite so hard.

# From Prosthetics to Platinum: A Candid Chat About Transformation

*Our beauty columnist sits down with the versatile character actress whose credits span the fantastical world of "Hellboy II: The Golden Army" to the comedic suburbs of "Kath and Kim"*

---

There's something refreshingly honest about actresses who've spent hours in a makeup chair being transformed into someone—or something—entirely different. When you've had your face reshaped with foam latex and worn fantasy contact lenses, you develop a certain perspective on beauty that most people never reach.

That's exactly what I discovered when I sat down to talk transformation, hair color, and the physical demands of committing to a character.

## Going Platinum: "It Changes How People See You"

The conversation kicked off with her recent decision to go platinum blonde—a dramatic departure that had fans buzzing.

"Going platinum is a commitment, let me tell you," she laughed. "It's not just walking into a salon and walking out three hours later. It's the upkeep, the toner, the deep conditioning treatments because that level of lightening is hard on your hair."

She offered practical wisdom for anyone considering the leap: "You have to be prepared for the maintenance. I keep a purple shampoo in rotation to fight brassiness, and I've become obsessed with bond-building treatments. Your hair needs the extra love when you strip it that light."

But beyond the practical, she noted something deeper. "There's a psychology to it. Platinum reads as bold, almost armor-like. People approach you differently. As an actress, I find hair color is one of the fastest ways to signal a character's entire personality."

## Gaining Weight for a Role: "Beauty Standards Had to Go Out the Window"

When the topic turned to physical transformation for roles, she grew more reflective.

"Gaining weight for a part is one of the more misunderstood aspects of what we do," she explained. "There's this assumption it's easy—like you just eat cake and enjoy yourself. But doing it in a healthy, deliberate way, under supervision, is actually its own kind of discipline."

She emphasized the mental shift required. "You have to release your ego and your vanity. For that stretch of time, you're not chasing a magazine-cover version of beauty. You're serving the story. And honestly? It was freeing. I stopped scrutinizing myself in the mirror and started appreciating what my body could communicate on screen."

Her skincare, she noted, actually improved during those periods. "When you're not restricting, your skin sometimes thanks you. I had this glow I hadn't seen in years."

## The Art of Prosthetic Makeup: "Hours in the Chair"

No conversation with an actress from the "Hellboy" universe would be complete without discussing prosthetic work—the elaborate, hours-long process of becoming a creature in Guillermo del Toro's richly imagined world.

"Prosthetics are a masterclass in patience," she said, her eyes lighting up. "You're sitting in that chair before dawn while brilliant artists build a new face onto yours piece by piece. The application alone could take four or five hours."

She spoke with genuine admiration for the craftspeople involved. "These makeup artists are sculptors, painters, and engineers all at once. They understand facial anatomy better than most doctors. Watching them blend the edges of a prosthetic so it becomes invisible—it's pure artistry."

The experience, she said, taught her about skin from the inside out. "Wearing prosthetics all day, your skin needs recovery. The removal process, the adhesives—it can be harsh. I learned to double down on gentle cleansing and barrier-repair moisturizers. Every night after a shoot, my routine was about calming and restoring."

She paused, then added with a smile: "It also gave me endless respect for anyone's natural skin. After being encased in latex for twelve hours, feeling your own bare skin breathe again is the greatest luxury there is."

## Beauty as Transformation

What unites these experiences—the platinum hair, the weight fluctuations, the fantastical prosthetics—is a philosophy of beauty as something fluid rather than fixed.

"I don't think of beauty as one look," she reflected as our time wound down. "I've been a suburban comedy character, a fantasy creature, a platinum bombshell. Every version taught me something. Real beauty confidence comes from knowing you can transform and still be completely yourself underneath it all."

It's a lesson worth remembering the next time we hesitate before a bold change—whether that's a new hair color or simply embracing our own skin, exactly as it is.

---

*Interview edited for length and clarity.*
